title: Representation
oneLine: Preferred way of representing information and experience.
frontSummary: People organise experience through preferred sensory-symbolic channels: pictures, sounds, body sensations, or words.
definition: Representation describes how people take in external sensory information and reproduce it internally. A person may prefer to think in images, sounds, body sensations, or language.
languageCues: Visual: see, view, looks right, picture, show
Auditory: hear, sounds right, listen, tone, quiet
Kinaesthetic: feel, handle, sense, touch, move
Language: words, rules, criteria, lists, definitions
behaviouralSigns: Visual: looks upward, prefers diagrams, notices appearance
Auditory: attends to tone, rhythm, words, and sound
Kinaesthetic: gestures, slows down, references body feeling
Language: prefers reading, concepts, labels, and criteria
strengths: Helps tailor coaching, teaching, and communication
blindSpots: May miss information delivered in another format
May assume others process experience the same way
coachingPrompts: Do you need to see it, hear it, feel it, or put it into words?
What format makes this easiest for you to understand?
How are you representing this internally right now?
visualScene: A person choosing between four learning inputs: a picture, headphones, a physical object, and a book.
example: A visual client may understand a plan through a diagram, while a language-oriented client may prefer written criteria and steps.

title: Scale / Scope
oneLine: Preferred level of information: specifics, lateral links, or big picture.
frontSummary: People differ in whether they begin with details, the big picture, or sideways associations.
definition: Scale describes the size of information a person prefers when thinking, communicating, learning, and understanding. Some begin with specifics and build upward, some begin with the whole picture and move downward, while others think laterally through analogies and relationships.
languageCues: Detail: specifics, exactly, step-by-step, what specifically
Global: overall, big picture, principle, concept, purpose
Lateral: like, similar to, reminds me of, analogy, story
behaviouralSigns: Detail: asks for specifics before feeling clear
Global: wants the purpose or frame before the details
Lateral: connects ideas through stories, metaphors, and analogies
blindSpots: Detail: can get lost in complexity
Lateral: may wander away from the immediate task
coachingPrompts: Do you need the big picture first or the details first?
What level of detail would make this useful?
visualScene: Three people viewing the same project: one inspecting fine details, one viewing the whole map, and one connecting it to another idea with puzzle pieces.
example: In planning, a global thinker may ask why the project matters, while a detail thinker wants the exact next steps.

title: Motivation
oneLine: Direction of motivational energy: toward desired outcomes or away from unwanted outcomes.
frontSummary: People are motivated either by moving toward what they want or away from what they want to avoid.
definition: Motivation describes the direction of intent. Toward motivation is pulled by goals, gains, and possibilities. Away From motivation is driven by avoiding problems, risks, pain, or unwanted consequences.
languageCues: Toward: achieve, gain, create, reach, obtain, build
Away From: avoid, prevent, reduce, stop, get rid of, stay away from
behaviouralSigns: Toward: talks about goals, visions, and positive outcomes
Away From: notices risks, problems, consequences, and what could go wrong
strengths: Away From: risk awareness, prevention, quality control, contingency planning
blindSpots: Toward: may ignore risks or warning signs
Away From: may struggle to define positive goals
coachingPrompts: What will having this do for you?
What do you want to avoid?
What problem are you trying to prevent?
visualScene: One person walking toward a bright goal on a path, while another moves away from a warning sign and storm clouds.
example: A Toward client may be energised by a vision of success. An Away From client may take action once they clearly see the cost of staying the same.

title: Stress Coping
oneLine: How a person responds under pressure, threat, or stress.
frontSummary: People may move away from stress, think and choose through stress, or go at stress directly.
definition: Stress Coping describes how people perceive and respond when they feel threatened or pressured. Passive coping moves away from stress, assertive coping keeps presence of mind and chooses a response, and aggressive coping goes directly at the stressor.
languageCues: Passive: peace, avoid, keep harmony, should, must
Assertive: choose, pause, respond, think, decide
Aggressive: challenge, confront, take on, push through
behaviouralSigns: Passive: avoids conflict, seeks harmony, may people-please
Assertive: pauses, evaluates, chooses a response
Aggressive: confronts pressure directly, may intimidate or over-push
strengths: Passive: preserves peace and reduces escalation
Aggressive: brings courage, energy, and directness
blindSpots: Passive: can become avoidance or self-abandonment
Assertive: requires emotional regulation and awareness
Aggressive: can become controlling, reactive, or unsafe
coachingPrompts: When stressed, do you move away, pause and choose, or move toward the stressor?
What would an assertive response look like here?
What are you protecting yourself from?
visualScene: Three people facing a pressure situation: one stepping back, one calmly choosing, and one charging forward.
example: In conflict, a passive pattern may avoid the conversation, an assertive pattern may name the issue calmly, and an aggressive pattern may attack the problem or person.

title: Self-Esteem
oneLine: Whether self-worth is treated as earned or inherent.
frontSummary: Self-esteem concerns a person’s sense of worth as a human being.
definition: Self-Esteem describes how a person relates to their own worth. Conditional self-esteem links value to performance, approval, achievement, or external conditions. Unconditional self-esteem recognises worth as inherent.
languageCues: Conditional: I have to prove myself, I’m only valuable if, I need to earn it
Unconditional: I have worth, I matter, my value is not up for negotiation
behaviouralSigns: Conditional: overachieving, approval-seeking, shame after mistakes
Unconditional: steadier self-regard, more acceptance, less identity collapse after failure
strengths: Conditional: can drive performance and effort
Unconditional: supports resilience, dignity, and emotional stability
blindSpots: Conditional: can create perfectionism, people-pleasing, and chronic proving
Unconditional: may be misunderstood as avoiding accountability if not balanced with responsibility
coachingPrompts: Do you experience your worth as something you must earn?
What happens to your sense of self when you make a mistake?
What would change if your worth was not conditional on performance?
visualScene: A person looking into a mirror, with one side showing achievement trophies and the other showing calm self-acceptance.
example: A client with conditional self-esteem may feel valuable only when performing well. A client with unconditional self-esteem can still improve without making mistakes mean they are worthless.
